issues.legal_issue: A state financial corporation exercising statutory powers over a debtor’s property must act fairly, reasonably, and in good faith as a prudent trustee would act.
material_facts: The corporation took possession of property securing an industrial loan and proceeded to sell it under its statutory recovery powers.
The corporation was an instrumentality of the State, and the statutory scheme required it to hold and apply sale proceeds for the debtor’s benefit as well as its own recovery.
issues.conclusion: The corporation’s exercise of its statutory powers was subject to public-law standards of fairness, reasonableness, and good faith, and its duties in dealing with the property were analogous to those of a prudent trustee.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 24 and 29(4) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951 require the corporation to act on business principles with due regard to industry, commerce, and the general public, and treat it as holding recovered property and proceeds in trust for the debtor. Its public-law conduct must satisfy reasonableness and public-interest standards: Kasturilal Laxmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir. The corporation must exercise care comparable to a prudent owner or trustee in protecting the debtor’s property and securing the best reasonably obtainable price.

predicates.financial_corporation_exercises_recovery: A financial corporation exercises a statutory power to recover a loan from an industrial concern.
predicates.debtor_property_is_under_its_control: The corporation takes or exercises control over property belonging to, or securing the debt of, the debtor.

issues.definition: When a financial corporation exercises recovery powers over a debtor’s property, it must deal with that property fairly and reasonably.

issues.legal_issue: A loan default does not by itself justify taking over an industrial unit or recovering against its property where the corporation’s own failure to provide committed financing contributed to the unit’s inability to operate.
material_facts: The corporation sanctioned a loan but disbursed less than the sanctioned amount, without explaining its failure to release the balance.
The mill struggled because of inadequate working capital and lack of cooperation from other partners, and repayment defaults followed.
The corporation initiated recovery proceedings and took possession of the secured property.
issues.conclusion: The recovery action was not justified in the circumstances because the corporation had failed to release the full committed loan and the resulting shortage of capital contributed to the unit’s difficulties.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 permits recovery action following default, but default alone is insufficient to justify taking possession or selling property; those steps should be taken only when imperative and exercised fairly and reasonably. The purpose and business principles in Section 24 require efforts to make a unit viable and to accommodate difficulties affecting its ability to operate. The corporation should release its committed loan in time unless it has good reasons, communicated beforehand, for withholding it; recovery may not be justified where it fails to do so.

rule.if: financial_recovery_proceeding and loan_default and corporation_withheld_committed_financing and unit_operation_was_hampered_by_capital_shortage

predicates.financial_recovery_proceeding: A financial corporation brings a recovery proceeding against an industrial concern or its property.
predicates.loan_default: The industrial concern has failed to repay the loan or an instalment when due.
predicates.corporation_withheld_committed_financing: The corporation failed to disburse financing it had committed to provide and did not establish a good reason for withholding it.
predicates.unit_operation_was_hampered_by_capital_s: The industrial concern’s ability to start or continue operating was impaired by a shortage of working capital.

issues.definition: A recovery proceeding following default is not justified without a fair assessment when the corporation withheld committed financing and the resulting capital shortage hampered the unit’s operation.

issues.legal_issue: A financial corporation’s sale of a defaulting unit or secured property must be conducted fairly and in a manner that gives the debtor a meaningful opportunity to protect the property’s value and offer to pay the debt.
material_facts: The corporation invited tenders and accepted a tender after negotiation, allowing payment over time.
The accepted offer was substantially below the appellant’s earlier proposed payment in settlement, and the appellant was not given notice or an opportunity to respond before acceptance.
The sale was made without a fair opportunity for the appellant to submit an offer or bring forward a higher offer.
issues.conclusion: The sale was unjust and unreasonable, was vitiated, and was set aside; the corporation was directed to resume possession and, if it later sold the property, to do so by open auction with wide publicity.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 does not exclude natural justice. The corporation must act as a prudent trustee, seek competitive offers and the maximum reasonable price, and give the debtor relevant valuation and tender information and an opportunity to respond. Sale by public auction is the preferred method; a departure must be justified, and private negotiation is confined to exceptional large or specialised concerns with broad advertising. These requirements draw on Fertiliser Corporation Kamgar Union v. Union of India, Ram & Shyam Co. v. State of Haryana, Sachidanand Pandey v. State of West Bengal, Haji T.M. Hassan v. Kerala Financial Corporation, and Lakshmanasami Gounder v. C.I.T.

predicates.financial_corporation_sale_proceeding: A financial corporation sells a defaulting industrial unit or property securing a loan.
predicates.debtor_was_not_given_notice_or_opportuni: The corporation did not inform the debtor of the proposed acceptance or give the debtor an opportunity to respond or make an offer before the sale.
predicates.sale_process_was_not_fairly_competitive: The sale process did not fairly invite and assess competitive offers or otherwise reasonably seek the best available price.

issues.definition: A sale by a financial corporation must be set aside when the debtor was denied notice and an opportunity to respond and the process was not fairly competitive.

issues.legal_issue: A debtor’s request to release property not occupied by the industrial unit should normally be granted when its sale can help repay the loan.
material_facts: The appellant sought release of a vacant mortgaged plot to sell it together with other land and apply the proceeds toward the debt.
The plot was not occupied by the mill, and its release could enable a sale that might help discharge the arrears.
issues.conclusion: The corporation was directed to release the vacant plot subject to the sale proceeds being paid into the loan account, with time allowed for repayment; if the arrears were not paid, the property was to be sold by open auction after wide publicity.
issues.legal_principle: The court directed that a request to release property owned by the debtor and not occupied by the concern should normally be granted on condition that the sale proceeds are deposited in the loan account. This reflects the requirements of fairness, prudent management, and recovery in accordance with the business principles in Section 24 and the powers and duties under Section 29 of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951.

predicates.financial_recovery_proceeding: A financial corporation is taking recovery action against an industrial concern or its property.
predicates.debtor_owns_unoccupied_secured_property: The debtor owns secured property on which the industrial concern is not situated.
predicates.release_can_help_repay_debt: Releasing the property would enable its sale and application of the proceeds toward repayment of the debt.

issues.definition: When the debtor owns secured property not occupied by the concern and its release can help repay the debt, the property should normally be released on condition that its proceeds go toward the debt.
